rows.notes: The study is a literature review (titled 'Review Article'; stated as a literature survey of journals, reports and grey literature on water management in Tanzania). It reports no own data, experiment, survey or model runs. Drip irrigation is mentioned only once, in passing, as an efficient technology demanding high initial capital that rural villagers cannot afford [76]; no figures on water-use efficiency gains (40-70%) or drought-stable yields appear anywhere.

Review article with no primary data. The only yield-related statement about modern irrigation is a secondary claim that positive crop yield responses have been realised where modern irrigation approaches were adopted, citing [53] (a rainwater harvesting profitability study), not drip and not the study's own result. No evidence on stable yields under drought with drip irrigation.

Review article; no own data. Drought risk is discussed generally (farmers need adaptation strategies to reduce crop loss from drought) but nothing on drip irrigation maintaining yields under drought. Drip appears only as a technology whose capital cost is a barrier for rural villagers.

Review article; no own data. The study contains no statement linking drip irrigation to uniform nutrient distribution, productivity or soil health. Soil-related content concerns salinity in an over-irrigated rice scheme (citing [70]), mulching, terracing and agroforestry, none of which involves drip irrigation.

notes: The cited study is explicitly a narrative literature review of agricultural water management in Tanzania with no primary data; Q1 is 'no' for all rows. Drip irrigation is mentioned in a single sentence (section 3.1.2) about high upfront cost. None of the four claims (40-70% WUE gain, stable yields under drought, risk management, soil health) is addressed in the text. The citation appears to be misattributed by the citing review.
